title: Deeds and grace
hook: deeds shape the body we are given; grace opens the door

segments.voice: Yesterday, order and effort: everyone within the hukam, and still the Gurus ask us to strive. Your line was strive within the order. What small piece did you do, and what did you let go? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

Two words, side by side, in the fourth pauri of Japji. Karmi, nadri. In paraphrase, the line runs: by deeds comes the robe; by grace, the door of liberation. A robe and a door. It's an odd pair to put in one breath. A robe is something you're wrapped in: you wear it every day, it takes the shape of you. A door is something you can stand in front of for a very long time and never open with your own hand. Guru Nanak puts both in one short line, and today we live inside it. Today's word is the first half: karam.
screen: `A ROBE AND A DOOR.` → `KARMI, NADRI.` → `TODAY'S WORD: THE FIRST HALF.`

segments.voice: First, the robe. Sikh readers take the robe in this line as the body, the life we're given. Karam is deeds, actions and their weight. What we have done shapes what we carry: the body, the circumstances, the habits that wrap around us. That's the first half of the line, and on its own it would be a strict ledger. Second, the door. Nadar is the glance, the gracious look of the One. The line says the door of liberation opens by nadar, not by karam. You can do good for a lifetime, and the door is still not a thing you buy. It is given. Third, why both. If the line said only deeds, life would be bookkeeping, and anyone behind would stay behind. If it said only grace, there would be no reason to do good at all. Guru Nanak keeps both: deeds matter, they really do shape us, and the last step is a gift. The same pauri closes by saying, in paraphrase, that the True One is all of it. Fourth, how readers hold the line. Some Sikh interpreters read karmi itself as grace, so the robe, too, would be a gift. Others read it as deeds, as we've done today. Both readings keep grace at the door. So the Sikh life this points to looks like the farmer from yesterday: do the good that's in front of you, with your whole heart, and leave the door to the giver. Deeds and grace.
screen: `KARAM: DEEDS SHAPE THE ROBE.` · `NADAR: GRACE OPENS THE DOOR.` · `NOT A LEDGER, NOT AN EXCUSE.` · `DO THE GOOD; LEAVE THE DOOR.` · then, large: `DEEDS AND GRACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do a good deed, hope for grace. Settle, and breathe. Choose one good deed you can do today: carrying something for someone, a message to a person who's lonely, a bill paid fairly, a kind word to a coworker. Picture yourself doing it. Then let the picture end the moment the deed is done, and let the result belong to someone else. If you pray, you can turn that letting go into a hope for grace. If you don't, just feel the difference between doing and receiving. The bell holds the time.
Karam. Deeds, actions and their weight: in Japji, by deeds comes the robe, and by grace, nadar, the door of liberation. Today's word.
Your line: deeds and grace. Today, do the good deed you chose, then let it go without counting it, and leave the door to the One. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning, including the line about deeds and the robe, grace and the door, and Sikh life joins seva and honest work with remembrance and trust in the Guru's grace.

trapdoor: what you thought: karam is a cosmic scoreboard, and you get what you earn.
what it means: deeds shape the robe, the life we carry; grace opens the door.
what a scholar hears: readers differ on karmi in Japji's fourth pauri, deeds or grace, and both readings keep the door as a gift.

notes: Paraphrase of 'karmee aavai kaprraa nadree mokh duaar' (Japji pauri 4) and the pauri's close 'Nanak evai jaaneeai sabh aape sachiaar'; please confirm both paraphrases.
The reading of 'kaprraa' (robe) as the body follows the outline's hook; please confirm.
The note that some interpreters read 'karmi' as grace (Persian karam) and others as deeds is stated without naming anyone; please confirm it is fair, and whether to name the readings.
No etymology of karam is argued; the trapdoor stays with readings of the line.
Editor: corrected the paraphrase of pauri 4's close ('sabh aape sachiaar': the True One is all, not 'knows everything'); replaced the open-palms gesture, which repeated day 1354's practice.
